Cditot J Pteamble 


Success cannot be reckoned in gold 
alone. The results of our conference 
give ample proof to the adage. Only 
a few short weeks ago we closed the 
doors on 1954*s meetings and work* 
shops sponsored by the Canadian 
Camping Association. Admittedly, not 
one of us underestimates the value of 
a? profit column, but it seems that we 
wait with bated breath during the 
balancing-off period until its totals 
reach a so-call^ suitable figure. 

That is all very well. But this year 
another form of profit has increased 
our stature. Letters and post-mortem 
conversations applaud our most grati¬ 
fying gain as an intangible: goodwill 
and a general feeling of good fellow¬ 
ship, both of which pervaded meeting 
and meal. Workshop and seminar . . . 
even the registraticoi desk, they tell us! 

Kindred Group Luncheons afforded 
a place of discussion and hospitality to 
many delegates, a good number of 
whom could not otherwise have 
attended the Conference. It is a dis¬ 
tinct tribute to the chairmen of the 
ten individual divisions that by their 
tireless efforts they were able to en¬ 
courage twenty to thirty members to 
attend each luncheon group. High 
enthusiasm called for a repeat perform¬ 
ance next year, and you can be very 
sure that the committee has already 
earmarked both luncheon periods for 
that purpose. 

To Bert Danson, Dave Palter and 
Howard Glaze, Cliff Labbett and Bill 
Chapman, Barry Lowes and C. T. 


Sharpe and all those who were^in any 
way connected with operations, these 
comments from delegates speak for 
themselves: 

“Your committee has given this con¬ 
ference a professional finish . . .” 

“I cannot remember attending a con¬ 
ference where I have gained so much 
background information and ‘know¬ 
how’ ”. 

“As a newcomer to this country and 
to the Association, I am most impressed 
by the value packed into panels and 
discussion groups”. 

From our U.S. visitors, this superb 
compliment: “We feel as much at 
home here as we did at our own 
Conference in New York.” 

Next year’s Conference dates, by the 
way, will be February 24, 25 and 26, 
1955. 

Our sights are set at a high level for 
the next few years. Through an up¬ 
surge in interest and general support, 
we feel we are on the verge of 
expansion. CCA has many new mem¬ 
bers who had never heard of us in the 
past. We, at the core of the organiza¬ 
tion, look over the horizon to green 
pastures soon to be reached, we hope, 
where the office outgrows its present 
quarters, when an increased staff exists 
for the express purpose of giving better 
service and more individual help to a 
vast membership, and when a confer- 

(continued page 39).

Camping Ethics 

John Hoyle 

Directorf Camp GayVenture 


We who are camp directors have 
many, and perhaps increasing, prob¬ 
lems to consider. One is that we must 
in all and every sense act and maintain 
standards in our dealings with each 
other, our staffs, and parents, on the 
very highest level. True, camps may 
be run primarily as business ventures 
or primarily as service ventures, but 
in either and all cases, we who by 
choice or appointment are in charge 
of camps must constantly be checking 
ourselves to be sure that, in the words 
of Scripture, we “provide things honest 
in the sight of all men”. 

Whether we like it or not (and most 
of us don’t there is keen competition 
for both staff members and campers. 
The writer knows from experience how 
very easy it is, with the pressures under 
which we live, to take some slight 
advantage which, when reviewed in 
the light of day, may not be absolutely 
above board. 

Camping is an ideal, it is a standard, 
it is the demonstration of living on 
the highest level. There is, therefore, 
thrust upon us a requirement that we 
cannot dodge, even if we wished to, 
of maintaining our ethical behaviour 
at a level utterly above any voice of 
criticism. 

It might help all of us to re-read 
very carefully the “Business Principles 
of the Ontario Camping Association”, 
which were adopted some years ago 
and which are still our daily guide. 


These Principles or “Code of Ethics” 
suggest certain areas to which each of 
us as Camp Directors should give our 
very careful attention. 

It is, perhaps, unnecessary to reiter¬ 
ate what is already in the Code directly 
or by inference, but it may help to 
clarify our thinking if we consider two 
or three of these: 

1. Directors need to have confidence 
in each other. There are many ways 
in which they can share any special 
ideas or achievements with others. 
There is no doubt that all will benefit 
more by co-operation than by competi¬ 
tion. 

2. Directors need to be very, very 
careful in their approach to staff and 
campers. Persons known to have been 
at another camp the previous year 
should never be approached. If an 
approach comes from a staff member, 
then the director of the previous camp 
should be communicated with before 
any negotiations for a new contract 
are made. 

3. Bidding up on honoraria is 
another cause of misery, trouble and 
heartache. The writer hopes the time 
may come when some common stand¬ 
ards for honoraria may be reached. 
This would be a difficult thing to do 
when conditions vary so much, but 
some such mutual arrangement would 
work wonders in smoothing out some 
of the hard feelings that have some¬ 
times arisen between directors. So, is 
it too much to hope that in this field 


8 


Canadian Camping 


as in others, we endeavour to practice 
that ideal standard, the Golden Rule? 

4. The scrupulous adherence to 
contracts, verbal or written, between 
Director and Staff, is another factor 
to which attention needs be given. 
(The writer is aware that a verbal 
contract is not worth the paper it is 
written on (!!) but the principle 
remains.) 

5. Questions of extras at camps are 
hot always made sufficiently clear to 
parents, in advance, resulting in bad 
personal relations not only to the camp 
involved but to the whole camping 
movement. 

This article, which has been sub¬ 
mitted to several camp directors for 
approval before publishing, is presented 
in deep humility, with the knowledge 
that it is so easy for anyone to err, 
and in the hope that when difficulties 
do occur they be brought- before a 
committee of the Association to be 
settled privately and without publicity. 
It is not written in the spirit of criti¬ 
cism, but only with the hope of assist¬ 
ing to maintain those grand principles 
which have made Canadian Camping 
something of which Canadians are 
justly proud. 


Business Principles in the O. C. A. 

1. A director should actively affiliate 
himself with the professional organiza¬ 
tions in the Camping Field. 

2. Directors and counsellors should 
be willing to assist other directors and 
counsellors by giving such information 
and advice as they can impart without 
detriment to themselves or their work. 

3. It is unprofessional for a director 
knowingly to take the initiative in 
negotiating \yith any counsellors, in¬ 


structors or employees, who, during 
th preceding summer, wpre associated 
with another camp, without consulting 
the director of the other camp, in tne 
spirit of good will; or for the first 
director to carry on such negotiations 
after a counsellor has signed up else¬ 
where. 

It is, also unprofessional for a director 
knowingly to take the initiative in 
negotiating with a propective camper 
who, during the preceding season, was 
at another camp; or to carry on nego¬ 
tiations with a camper who has already 
been enrolled elsewhere. 

4. It is unprofessional for a director 
to enter, with the parent of a camper, 
into a secret or confidential agreement 
of such a nature as would result in the 
loss of the good will of the parents of 
the other campers, were the conditions 
of the agreemnt to become known.^ 
This provision is to be construed in 
order to prevent price cutting in direct 
competition with other camps, but not 
to prevent camps from giving bona 
fide scholarships. A scholarship is to 
be interpreted as being an honorarium' 
granted by the camp director to a 
camper because of the inability of the 
parents to pay the customary fees. 

5. It is professional to use as refer¬ 
ences only those people who have 
reliable knowledge of the camp or the 
director, preferably both. 

6. It is unethical for a camp to 
advertise in its prospectus, any activ-.- 
ity or service for which it does not 
provide adequate leadership and facili¬ 
ties. 

7. If, in spite of the acceptance of 
this set of Business Principles, compli¬ 
cations should arise, members should 
report the matter to the Board, and 
refrain from discussing same outside 
the Association. 


Torontoj Canada, April, 1954

AMONG OURSELVES . . . 

c4» cQ* Cockxane 

Director, Gamp Temagami 


We still sadly miss our old friend 
Ernest Arthur Chapman, who died sud¬ 
denly, following a heart attack, several 
years ago. “Ernie” Chapman was a 
man of unusual ability, strong charac¬ 
ter and forceful yet genial personality. 
One of his outstanding qualities was 
his exhuberant cheerfulness, and his 
irrepressible humour infected all with 
whom he came into contact. He was 
truly beloved by a host of friends. 

Born in Hamilton sixty-nine years 
ago, Mr. Chapman received his early 
education there. He was for several 
years physical instructor at old High- 
field School, Hamilton. In 1905 he was 
appointed physical director of Saint 
Andrew’s College; this position he held 
for over thirty years. 

Ernest Chapman and Miss Leila 
K i r k b r i d e , affectionately known as 
“Fernie”, of Hamilton were married 
in 1909: three daughters and one son 
survive their father. The girls are 
Miriam, now Mrs. K. S. Moeser; Helen 
(Mrs. R. W. Mitchell) and Catherine 
{Mrs. E. S. Smith). William R. Chap¬ 
man, the only son, is well known to 
the Camping Association. 

Brimming with an irresistible sense 
of humour and high spirits, Ernie was 
an inveterate practical joker-—with his 
friends and, at times, perfect strangers 
as his victims. These frequently 
reciprocated with payment in kind. 
Whether the instigator or himself the 
butt of these sallies, it made no differ¬ 
ence, for he also thoroughly enjoyed 
the situation when the tables were 
tumc^d against him. His whimsical 
smile and obvious lack of guile carried 
him through situations where otherwise 
offence might have been taken. 


Limited space prevents a recital of 
many of his puckish outbursts. He and 
I were close neighbours and intimate 
friends for many, many years, and met 
almost daily to talk over camp affairs 
and our mutual interests in certain 
Canadian mines. Shortly before his 
death, and while out walking, I met 
Ernie, and I quote his characteristic 
salutation: “Hello, Methuselah, are 
you still wandering about this Vale of 
Tears; don’t you realize there is a 
shortage of food in the world and that 
better men than you are going hungry; 
why don’t you shuffle off?” To this 
grim remark I asked Ernie what course 
he would advise me to take. His 
answer was, “You might be useful as 
fertilizer for^'a bed of dandelions 6' x 
3'.” As I had no gun he was allowed 
to go free. As we parted Ernie turned 
and with an abrupt change in manner 
said rather sadly, “I shall not live to 
be the age that you are today, but if 
the kids and the dogs on this street 
miss me, my life will not have been 
altogether wasted.” 

At a Convention dinner at the 
Y.M.C.A. several years ago, many 
campers will remember the amusement 
caused when a well known lady, the 
director of a pioneer girls’ camp and 
former editor of “Canadian Camping”, 
mislaid her fur coat in the auditorium. 
The coat was found and handed over 
to Ernie for return. As an old friend, 
here was an opportunity for exploita¬ 
tion. He therefore interrupted the pro¬ 
gramme and, standing on his chair, 
with the coat in full view, remarked, 
“This lady’s coat was left in the men’s 
washroom; will the owner please stand 
up.” Amid a gale of laughter, the 
garment was reclaimed. 


10 


Canadian Camping 


Although my junior by only thirteen 
yearSj Ernie sometimes introduced me 
to strangers as his father. Upon one 
such occasion and after a game of golf, 
he chose a promising-looking prospect. 
Following the formal introduction, he 
took his newly found acquaintance 
aside in the,club house to relate in a 
perfectly audible stage whisper the 
physical and mental deficiencies of his 
“poor old Dad’’. “He suffers from the 
delusion that he is a golfer, when 
marbles in the gutter is about his 
limit.” Meeting this person again, 
some few days later, the man remarked, 
“I see your father is not with you 
to-day.” “My father,” said Ernie in 
amazement, “whatever do you mean? 
He died over forty years ago!” Ernie, 
when relating the incident to me, said 
“I must improve my memory and my 
technique before I can aspire to 
become a really accomplished liar.” 

Becoming keenly interested in the 
educational and recreational value of 
organized camping, Mr. Chapman 
chose a site on Balsam Lake for Camp 
Kagawong more than forty years ago. 
He was actively engaged as director 
of this camp until the time of his 
death. It is of interest to note that 
Mr. William R. Chapman has suc¬ 
ceeded his father as director of Camp 
Kagawong. The many friends of this 
camp will wish a continuation of its 
success under his leadership. 

Interested in all forms of physical 
education, Mr. Chapman, Sr., after 
some years of preliminary work and 
planning, was one of several charter 
members responsible for the formation 
of the Ontario Branch of The Royal 
Life Saving Society, in 1908. He was 
an active worker in the Society; 
secretary-treasurer of the Ontario 
Branch for five years, and president 
from 1928. to 1934. He was also past 
president of the Ontario Camping 
Association. 


Those present at the last annual 
meeting of the Ontario Branch of the 
R.L.S5. attended by Mr. Chapman, 
will recall, with a sigh, the happy 
occasion when he personally made the 
first presentation of the Chapman Cup 
to a representative of Gamp Oconto. 
This annual 'award will serve to per¬ 
petuate the name of our friend. 

A many-sided man of rare quality, 
E. A. Chapman once held the title, for 
his weight, of Amateur Canadian 
Champion in both boxing and wrest¬ 
ling. A tireless worker in service to 
others, he was invariably sympathetic, 
understanding and kindly. He never 
failed to give ^ practical help or sound 
advice where needed. 

The radiant personality of Ernest 
A. Chapman inspired all with whom 
he came into contact. We think, of 
him not with tears but with a smile. 
May God rest his soul. 



ERNEST ARTHUR CHAPMAN 


Toronto^ Canada, Aprils 1954 


11 



School Camping 

in the United States 

Julian W. Smith 

Associate Professor, Outdoor Education 
School of Education, Michigan State College 
East Lansing, Michigan 


Few would deny that camping is 
one of the most popular forms of out¬ 
door activity. It is an old and accepted 
custom of living in the out-of-doors. 
Organized camping has been in exist¬ 
ence in the United States for nearly a 
century, and for a long time has been 
regarded as educational in character. 
It is only in comparatively recent years, 
however, that school camping has 
developed as an integral part of the 
curriculum of many schools. This more 
recent development in education, 
whereby a camp environment is used 
as a part of a classroom experience for 
children and teachers, is a part of the 
emerging community school program. 
Educational leaders, seeking more 
opportunities to provide real and direct 
learning experiences for children, have 
found that many things can be learned 
best in a camping situation. The 
acceptance of this principle by edu¬ 
cators, coupled with the popularity of 
camping by the public, has given 
impetus to the development of a sub¬ 
stantial number of school camping pro¬ 
grams throughout the United States. 

Another influence that has hastened 
the advent of school camping is the 
change in the mode of living. City 
dwelling and the machine age in the 
Mid-century period have accentuated 
the need for simple living. The concern 
about the wise use of natural resources 
has also made it seem important that 
people should have contact with the 
land. The unfolding program of school 
camping gives promise of providing 


for an ever-increasing number of chil¬ 
dren a short but effective living experi¬ 
ence in the out-of-doors as a part of 
school education. The use of the camp 
for educational experiences in no way 
duplicates or conflicts with the many 
excellent programs of organized camp¬ 
ing in which approximately 11% of 
the children in the United States 
participate each year. 

The Development of School Camping 

It is difficult to say just when camp¬ 
ing experiences began to find their way 
into the school program. Camping in 
the United States seemed to go through 
various stages, beginning with a recrea¬ 
tional emphasis, but tending more and 
more to be regarded as educational as 
time went on. 

In 1861, Frederick William Gunn, 
who is often regarded as the founder 
of organized camping in the United 
States, and who was head of the 
gunnery school for boys in Washington, 
Connecticut, took the student body for 
a two-weeks’ trip into the out-of-doors. 
Since that time, other camping pro¬ 
grams related to the school have been 
reported, but usually it was the case 
of a school group’s going to camp 
under the sponsorship of some other 
agency, such as a recreation depart¬ 
ment or a youth serving organization. 
These programs usually took place dur¬ 
ing the summer months. Such a pro¬ 
gram is reported in Los Angeles, 
California, in the mid-twenties. 


12 


Canadian Camping 



In Michigan, the Tappan Junior 
High School, Ann Arbor, developed a 
camp through community interests, and 
short trips to the new location soon 
became a regular part of the school 
year. This was in the early thirties. 
About the same time in Cadillac, 
Michigan, the board of education ac¬ 
quired property, constructed buildings, 
and operated a camp during the sum¬ 
mer months for children of element¬ 
ary school age. Many other schools 
have used camp for such activities, 
but not as a regular part of the school 
program. In the literature about camp¬ 
ing, reference is often made to the 
desirability of camping under the 
auspices of schools. With the establish¬ 
ment of Life Camps in the thirties, 

L. B. Sharp, Director, began to en¬ 
courage school camping. It was not 
until 1940, however, that the first year- 
round camp went into operation on the 
assumption that school camping should 
be an integral part of the curriculum. 
This first camp was made possible by 
the W. K. Kellogg Foundation of 
Battle Creek, Michigan. The Clear 
Lake Camp and staff were made avail¬ 
able to three Michigan schools—Battle 
Creek-Lakeview (of which the writer 
was Principal at that time), Decatur, 
and Otsego—for one year. Students 
from grades four to twelve went to 
camp for two-week periods, and the 
new venture was so successful that the 
schools of Calhoun County, including 
Battle Creek, initiated a similar pro¬ 
gram in the early forties. 

In 1945, the Michigan Superintend¬ 
ent of Public Instruction (Eugene B. 
Elliott) initiated a demonstration re¬ 
search program of school camping and 
outdoor education in co-operation with 
the Department of Conservation and 
the W. K. Kellogg Foundation. The 
program was later carried forward 
under the leadership of the late Lee 

M. Thurston who succeeded Dr. Elliott 
as Michigan’s Superintendent of Public 
Instruction. Hugh B. Masters, then 


Educational Director of the W. K. 
Kellogg Foundation, and the late P. J. 
Hoffmaster, Director of the Michigan 
Department of Conservation, both 
leaders with great social vision, gave 
invaluable service in the development 
of outdoor education. It was the 
writer’s privilege to direct this experi¬ 
mental venture, which, during a period 
of seven years, resulted in upwards of 
100 school districts in Michigan having 
developed school camping programs. 
The most extensive of these are Dear¬ 
born and Battle Creek Public Schools, 
which now operate on a year-round 
basis. Many others, however, now 
provide school camping over a period 
of several weeks and months. The pro¬ 
gram in Michigan has had public 
endorsement in the form of an act 
passed by the Legislature in 1945 which 
enables school districts to acquire 
camps and operate them as a part of 
the regular educational and recrea¬ 
tional program of the schools. In 1949, 
the Legislature set aside funds in the 
State School Aid Bill to encourage 
secondary schools to initiate camping 
programs. This plan is still in effect. 

The camping experience has great 
value to all groups. For children in 
the upper elementary grades to go to 
camp as a part of the educational

LIMITED TORONTO

experience for that age group is a 
logical and natural development. Ob- 
viously^ the problems of organization 
and administration are simpler in the 
elementary school. On the other hand, 
a strong case can be made for the 
junior high school with its exploratory 
functions, and there is little doubt that 
the traditional secondary program 
needs the vitalizing and freshening 
influence of the camping program. 
Experience in Michigan has demon¬ 
strated that the interest and enthusiasm 
of secondary school students are equal 
to that of any other age group, and 
the values appear to be just as 
significant. 

In the elementary school camp, much 
stress is placed on exploratory trips 
throughout the camp area, cook-outs, 
shelter construction, trail building, the 
use of the compass, and a great variety 
of other skills that have meaning and 
interest to children. For those of 
secondary school age, specific projects 
to improve the camp community have 
great interest — such as building of 
shelters, improving the park, timber 
management, studies and activities in 
game and fish management, and cor¬ 
rection of soil erosion. Interspersed 
with all of these are the trips and 
explorations to points of interest, such 
as marshes, quaking bogs, glacial lakes, 
sand dunes, high cliffs, desert areas, 
tropical swamps, sawmills, and gravel 
pits. Appropriate activities depicting 
the folklore and history of the area are 
also unique in camping. Indian life, 
lumbering, mining, transportation, and 
land management are illustrations. 

There will be in each instance the 
arts and crafts associated with the 
native materials. Among these will be 
making and using archery equipment, 
basket weaving, excavation of Indian 
relics, painting, music, poetry, and 
dramatics, which come only through 
the natural and unhibited interests of 
children. 


14 


CANADIAN Camping 











Sch&^i Camping 

in Canada 

Catherine Sgholes 

Formerly Head of the Department of Health and Physical Education, 
York Memorial Collegiate Institute 


School camping is a comparatively 
new development in education. It is 
an extension of education to the out-of- 
doors. It takes place in school time and 
is an integral part of the school cur¬ 
riculum. It attempts to do those things 
which are best done outside the class¬ 
room. It vitalizes classroom education. 

In countries such as the United . 
States, Great Britain, Finland and 
Germany, school camping has been 
seriously experimented with for 'over 
two decades. In some regions it has 
reached national importance. It has 
been officially recognized and subsidized 
so that it can be a part of the rightful 
experience of children, whatever their 
financial status. Because' of its intrinsic 
educational significance and its value 
as a complement to the school curricu¬ 
lum, in many areas it has become a 
part of the year-round programme of 
the school. 

How have we in Canada participated 
in this growing educational venture? 
To us, too, the idea of school camping 
is not entirely new, although it has only 
recently been actively carried into effect. 
Here, as in the United States, it prob¬ 
ably began with recreation. Over the 
years, enthusiastic teachers have taken 
groups of students on ski or camping 
trips or travelled with them to places 
of interest in holiday time. The un¬ 
limited educational opportunities of 
such ventures soon became apparent. 
Spurred on, also, by the experiences 


of those who had elsewhere experi¬ 
mented in and established school 
camps, we in Canada made a begin- 
ing. In Ontario four schools have 
pioneered in school camping within 
the last four years. Upon investigation 
we find that no other province in 
Canada has school camps. 

In 1950, a small group of preparatory 
school boys from Pickering College, 
Newmarket, with three Grade 7 boys 
from Forest Hill Junior High School, 
Forest Hill Village, and the John Ross 
Robertson Public School, Toronto, to¬ 
gether with their masters, instituted the 
first school camp. Pickering College 
and Forest Hill have continued the 
project each year since. In 1951 the 
number of participating students 
doubled, each school taking about 
twenty-two boys. In 1952 and 1953 the 
two schools camped separately. The 
number of students from each school 
was increased, Pickering College experi¬ 
menting with Grade 7 and 8 boys. 
Forest Hill, with over seventy students 
throughout Grade 7, established co¬ 
educational camping. These were six- 
day camps and took place in March 
and late in April. 

In 1952, King George School, 
Guelph, began school camping with a 
class of forty Grade 5 boys and girls 
under the leadership of their classroom 
teacher. This was repeated the follow¬ 
ing year with an increase to seventy 
pupils. Each of these camps was a week 
long and was held in June.. 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1954 


15 




At the High School level, York 
Memorial Collegiate Institute, York 
Township, made its first camping ex¬ 
periment in 1953. A complete class¬ 
room unit of Grade 9 students, together 
with their home-room teacher, par¬ 
ticipated in a two-and-a-half-day co¬ 
educational camping experience in 
May. 

It is interesting to note that within 
these four schools, camping has been 
undertaken in spring, early summer and 
winter;- it has been a 11 e in p t e d at 
Elementary, Junior High and High 
School levels; and it has been tried 
by both residential and government 
schools. 

It was timely that at the onset of 
school camping in Ontario, the Depart¬ 
ment of Education was urging the study 
of conservation in the schools. This 
became the pivotal point around which 
all the camps centred. All camps had 
several aims,, namely, to further an 
appreciation of our national wealth and 
our need to conserve it; to widen 
horizons as pupils discover completely 
new ways of life; to improve skills for 
living and working with a social group; 
and to aid school learning, by providing 
an environment rich in real learning 
situations to make the classroom work 
more meaningful. 

The areas of conservation studied and 
the methods of learning depended 
partly upon such factors as the choice 



of camp site, the time of year, the 
length of the camp, the leadership 
available, and the ^:*ade level. The 
type of camp was further conditioned 
by specific school objectives, by the 
financial assistance given, and by where 
the emphasis was placed in the indi¬ 
vidual school camps. 

Forest Hill Junior High School and 
Pickering College chose Limberlost 
Lodge, near Huntsville. In these camps, 
emphasis was placed on the study of 
the natural resources of a northern 
country of lakes and woodland, and 
what has been happening to them over 
the years. The King George School 
camping projects took place at the 
Lutheran Church Camp in Wedgewood 
Park near Guelph. No overall topic 
was stressed in these camps, the sub¬ 
jects studied being related to the en¬ 
vironment rather than to a central 
theme. The York Memorial Collegiate 
students went to the Humber Glen 
Camp near Bolton. Here they studied 
the Humber Valley Conservation Area 
and how the Humber Valley Conserva¬ 
tion Authority is attempting to care for 
it. 

After preparatory academic work, 
conservation and its allied subjects 
became part of the students* pro¬ 
gramme. Notebook supervision en¬ 
couraged them in their study of 
weather, birds, plants and animals, and 
it was only natural that after a six 
weeks’ study of world conservation, the 
classes investigated this field at the local 
level. 

Some questions arise, however, from 
these camping experiments. Does school 
camping not conflict with or encroach 
upon private and agency summer 
camps? What happens to the classes 
students miss by going to camp? Why 
did my child miss this camping ex¬ 
perience? School and summer camps 
should not conflict, but rather the one 
should benefit the other. Teachers and 
students with summer camp experience 
are valuable as leaders in the camp 
school. Pupils who have had a taste of 


16 


Canadian Camping 



school camping are enthusiastic pro¬ 
moters of the camping idea and want 
all the more to go to camp. Glasses 
missed by students at camp provide no 
real problem, as the camp learnings are 
fitted into the curricular studies of 
school. In schools where the entire 
class did not go to camp, the students 
remaining were absorbed by other 
classes of the same grade. School camp¬ 
ing is not available for all students in 
the school because so little camping has 
yet been attempted. But there are other 
reasons too. For some the cost is a 
problem. School camping can never 
reach all students until it has become 
an organized and subsidized part of the 
regular school curriculum. 

Is it desirable to introduce this type 
of education into our schools? It would 
seem that without school camping we 
are missing the best opportunity of pro¬ 
viding our youth with vital and dynamic 
educational experiences. Moreover, we 
are robbing them of the best possible 


medium for developing as peace-minded 
citizens. In camping can be found an 
enhancement of the joy, dignity and 
importance of work. 

Ontario’s school camping has become 
a^ reality through the co-operation of 
principals and teachers, parents, and 
pupils, local Boards of Education, and 
Home and School Associations, the 
Department of Education and various 
departments of our government, volun¬ 
tary leaders, interested citizens and 
tradespeople. But this formidable array 
of resources is not enough to enable 
school camping to become a national 
or even a province-wide experience. - 

Canada has the resources, facilities 
and the personnel to bring school camp¬ 
ing to our youth. How long will it be 
before all our assets are mobilized 
toward this end? And who will give 
leadership to further these vital and 
dynamic educational experiments? Will 
it be ourselves, members of* the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Association?

Listen to Learn 


Margaret Govan 
Director, Camp Ottawa 


It was a hot July day, and we were 
about to start on a nature walk^ seven 
nine- and ten-year-olds and myself. 
We had a- goal in view: to find a yellow 
birch and fasten a name to it so that 
those who walked along the path 
might absorb some painless learning 
. . , but the enthusiasm for marking 
trees was not at its highest peak. The 
•path wa-s narrow and we had to walk 
single file, which separated us con¬ 
siderably. The front five were Indians 
stalking Indians; the last two and 
myself were watching for a yellow 
birch. Of course we saw some other 
things, such as shrub honeysuckle with 
orange and yellow flowers on the same 
stem. 

“Do you know, I think that wild 
flowers are every bit as pretty as 
garden ones?** Eleanor confided. “I 
love them,’* and she stroked the petals, 
while Marian watched her. 

Coming up: one naturalist, I thought 
hopefully. ' 

But before we could inspect the 
flower further, the Indians had re¬ 
turned with wild whoops. “Have you 
found the tree yet? We’re hot.” 

“Not yet.” 


“Is it the kind of birch you make 
canoes out of?” Pat demanded. 

“No, stupid,” Ellen told her, and 
started a long tale of how the Indiaps 
made their canoes: she’d seen a movie. 
She was right too, and we had to find 
a bass wood and a spruce and a cedar 
before she’d finished, because she y 
rattled off all the names. 

“Where is this yellow birch?” Pat 
asked while,Ellen was recovering her 
breath. 

“There is one just beyond the fork 
in the path, to the left,” I told them. 

“Fork? Did somebody leave a fork? 
May I take it back to camp?” asked 
Joan eagerly. 

The others roared with laughter, and 
she.blushed scarlet. She ha-s had very 
little to do with adults and books are 
not .her strong point. I wonder how 
much teasing is going on in that cabin: 

I shall have to take steps. 

But Eleanor had an arm over Joan’s 
shoulder. “It’s what they call a divide 
in a path . . . see, like this. It would 
be a good word for ‘coffee-pot’ some¬ 
time.” 

We had reached the point and the 
tree, and we all sat down with one 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1954 


19 




accord, except Pat who was to attach 
the white-enameled, blacklettered top 
from a can, to the trunk. She did this 
with the critical help of the other six. 
Then we watched the water, which was 
moving sleepily in the sunshine. 

“Doesn’t it look wonderful!” said 
someone, speaking for everybody. 

I glanced at them: all seven were 
good swimmers, I was a qualified life¬ 
guard: and I knew this particular bit 
of shore. 

“When youVe cooler you can go in 
for a dip,” T told them. 

There was wild cheering, but it was 
too hot to make much of an effort, 
so we watched the water again. 

Evidently Joan’s eyes travelled fur¬ 
ther afield than the water. “Did you 
know that there are more greens than 
one?” she asked. “Simmie showed us 
yesterday when we were drawing, and 
there are lots and lots of them.” She 
pointed across to the wooded shore. 

“I know,” Eleanor nodded, sym- 
patheticallly. 

But the others were properly im¬ 
pressed. 

“Show me,” ordered Barbara, and 
Joan did. 

One up for Joan, I thought: perhaps 
I had begun worrying too soon. 

“See that spider web,” Marcia 
exclaimed and everybody jumped to 
her feet. Ellen gave a lecture on 
spiders, and it was a good one, trans¬ 
lated into junior language: they were 
all much impressed. 

Then they swam for their three 
minutes: they would be swimming 
again within the hour so I didn’t feel 
too hard-hearted. 


“The water against your skin . . . 
cool . . . like silk . . . lovely!” Mary 
exclaimed. 

As they were dressing, Eleanor eyed 
me seriously. “Would you mind telling 
me,” she said in her politest tone, 
“why God made mosquitoes?” 

I shook my head. “I don’t know.” 

‘T do,” said Pat as she pulled her 
T shirt over her head. I waited, not 
too expectantly. Pat’s legs are her 
strongest point. “Same as our mothers 
and fathers. Can’t have our own way 
all of the time or we’d be spoilt.” 

The six others nodded: that made 
sense to them. 

“Are we the best camp?” Mary 
enquired, hopping up and down on 
one foot, trying to shake some water 
out of her ear. 

“What makes a good camp?” I 
parried. 

“The place; the food; the counsel¬ 
lors; the water . . .” the answers were- 
as varied as the children. 

“I guess it’s campers make a camp,” 
Eleanor remarked profoundly. 

“Are you the best campers ?” I asked 
with a twinkle. 

They thought again. 

“Sometimes,” Pat allowed. 

“Then I guess we are the best camp 
sometimes,” Eleanor grinned. 

“O!” said Pat and considered this 
for almost a minute. “Let’s get going. 
What are we waiting for . . 

We got going. Nature study? . . . 
not what I’d planned. What they had 
learned they had taught themselves. 
Human nature study . . . for me, yes. 
Decidedly.

Elizabeth Wardley Raymer 
Director, Camp Tanamakoon 


A few items to keep in mind^ 

directors all^ when planning your 

programme: 

Be Sure to allot time ior: 

A. All counsellors to— 

1. Pass the camp safety tests. 

2. Become familiar with the equip¬ 
ment at his disposal, and pre¬ 
pare it for use. 

B. Activity Heads— 

1. Instruct their assistants in uni¬ 
form teaching standards. 

2. Organize- their assistants into a 
smoothly functioning group. 

C. Section Heads— 

To familiarize cabin counsellors 

with their duties and responsibili¬ 
ties. 

Advance Planning 

A. Plan all details of the daily and 
and evening programmes for the 
first week of camp. 

B. Prepare in detail two “Rainy 
Day” programs. 

C. Draw up a tentative schedule 
for the main events of the 
season. 

D. Work out plans for the arrival 
of the campers, covering every 
conceivable detail. Do this so 
thoroughly that each counsellor 
will know exactly what to do 
from the moment the campers 
arrive until the first regular 
counsellors’ meeting. 


This is the Time for the Director to: 

A. Present his philosophy of camp¬ 
ing. 

B. Put forward the aims, objectives, 
and policies of the camp. 

C. Begin a series (to be continued 
throughout the season) encom¬ 
passing Principles of Teaching, 
How to know and understand 
the campers, How to achieve 
discipline, etc. 

Remembering that the pre-camp 
period presents a golden opportunity 
to create an awareness ^of group 
solidarity and build a staff morale 
which will grow throughout the sum¬ 
mer— 

A. With the new staff members 
together: 

1, Have question and answer ses¬ 
sions. 

2. Give them assurance to counter¬ 
act the feeling of being the one 
untalented member of a group of 
experts. 

B. With the old staff members 
* together: 

1. Discuss their responsibilities to¬ 
ward the new members. 

2. Give them assurance that their 
past work has been appreciatecj- 

C. With the entire group present: 

1. Give adequate introductions, so 
that everyone will know about 
everyone else’s job.

Canadian Camping 










The Pre~Camp Conference 

... Am It Apptiem to Churt*h Campm 


Marjorie Goldsmith 

Camp Committee, Ontario Girls\ Work Board, OCCE 


Have you ever heard a camp leader 
wistfully sigh and exclaim at the end 
of a ten day camping period, “My, I 
wish I had received a little more train¬ 
ing before arriving at camp”? Most 
of us will admit that, either directly 
or indirectly, we have. Perhaps we 
have also wondered what to do about 
it. 

It is not at all peculiar to hear about 
Camp Committees which have difficul¬ 
ty in securing sufficient camp staff, let 
alone having leaders as well trained 
as they should be. There is certainly 
an urgent need to give our camp 
leaders training and help before they 
even set foot on camp. 

Camp Committees try to have camp 
staff arrive one or two days before 
the campers. This provides an op¬ 
portunity for staff to meet director, 
become familiar with the grounds, 
and make plans for camp programme. 

Camp leaders, no matter how cap¬ 
able they are in their own particular 
field — swimming, crafts, dramatics, 
Bible Study, etc. — feel the need for 
something more than the short, on-the- 
spot camp conference just before the 
campers arrive. It is important, there¬ 
fore, that some form of pre-camp 
training be planned for leaders of 
each camp. This is particularly essen¬ 
tial for the new and younger leaders 
and it will serve as a refresher for 
the more seasoned leader! 


When might such a pre-camp con¬ 
ference be held, you ask ? A great deal 
will depend upon locaf situations, but 
about six weeks to two months before 
the camp actually opens is a good time. 
A full day, with morning, afternoon, 
and evening sessions is really needed. 
Sometimes, however, leaders are able 
to be present just for the two sessions. 
It is a good plan to have at least one 
meal together, followed by a sing-song, 
of camp songs, or something else which 
may lend itself to the informal camp 
atmosphere. 

The number of topics it is possible 
to deal with in one day will need to 
be carefully chosen. Here are a few 
essentials: 

Often when we ask a person to be 
a camp leader we suggest that they do 
a specific job, and we forget to mention 
other duties they will be expected to 
carry out while at camp. It is not 
surprising that the leader is a little 
overwhelmed when she discovers sud¬ 
denly, at camp, her real role as a camp 
leader. At the pre-camp conference, 
there should be an opportunity to give 
a brief analysis of the leader’s duties, 
including specific jobs and other duties 
such as: supervising work groups dur¬ 
ing the camp period; assisting the 
swimming instructor as a land or boat 
patrol during camp; taking part in 
recreation programmes; helping with 
the planning of worship services; being 
counsellor of a cabin group. It is also 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1954 


23 



very necessary to help leaders become 
informed of the duties of the other 
staff members, such as the nurse, the 
business manager, the swimming in¬ 
structor. This will enable everyone to 
understand more clearly the impor¬ 
tance of working together in order to 
make the camp successful. The pur¬ 
poses and objectives of church camp¬ 
ing can be set forth very advantag¬ 
eously at this time, for it will give 
the leader an over-all picture of camp 
life and her part in helping to reach 
such goals. This important part of 
camp training is too frequently over¬ 
looked and, as a result, leaders fall far 
short of giving the effective Christian 
leadership which will enrich the lives 
of the boys and girls who come under 
their guidance. The leaders, them¬ 
selves, may have some very worthwhile 
suggestions to add to those already 
presented. One way toward reaching 
obectives at camp is to emphasize 
them at the pre-camp conference. 

In church camps where Bible Study 
is a part of the programme, leaders 


must prepare for leading such groups. 
A brief outline of the study book, 
methods of presentation and suggested 
projects which will help present the 
study in an attractive and interesting 
way, should find a place on the agenda 
of the pre-camp conference. Leaders 
will be given the help and incentive 
needed to prepare well for such leader¬ 
ship. 

Discussions on counselling and work¬ 
ing with campers in such matters as 
homesickness, discipline problems, 
group work techniques and others 
might very well be included in this 
training session. Some qualities of a 
good leader, such as self-discipline, 
co-operation, punctuality, wholesome 
attitudes, etc., are other suggestions 
for much needed discussions. 

The lecture method should be used 
just occasionally. Leaders should be 
given the opportunity for making sug¬ 
gestions and entering into discussions 
freely. In this way they will feel it is 
really “their” camp and doubtless will 
make more valuable contributions. 

This pre-camp conference for lead¬ 
ers is an important step ahead in pre¬ 
paring for good camp leadership. The 
material leaders receive before camp 
to help prepare for their job must take 
on new meaning and should. be more 
clearly understood because of the pre¬ 
camp conference experience. Leaders 
will go off to camp, when the time 
comes, more confident and desirous of 
being good leaders in the fullest sense 
of the word. 

The results are next to amazing. 
Try it.

Day Camp 

is Big Business 

Ivan Eaton_, Adult Programme Secretary 
Ottawa YMCA 


In Toronto alone, there are more 
than thirty Day Camps, involving over 
4,000 children for six to eight weeks 
of the summer and costing more than 
$40,000 to operate. However, in addi¬ 
tion to being big business, Day Camp 
is important business, because it deals 
with the physical health, the social and 
mental well-being of young children. 

Having as its goal, the social, educa¬ 
tional and physical development of the 
campers. Day Camping provides us 
the opportunity, but also the respon¬ 
sibility, of giving a satisfying, worth¬ 
while group experience in outdoor 
living. For this we need a good camp 
site, adequate equipment and facilities, 
but most important of all, a well 
trained staff. 

For the sake of this article, let us 
assume that the Camp Director is 
experienced, qualified and keen enough 
to avail himself of any opportunity to 
pool resources, exchange ideas and 
share problems with his fellow direc¬ 
tors. (Many metropolitan areas 
arrange director training courses, 
which are a boon to those responsible 
for Day Camp). 

Our prime interest then is the train¬ 
ing of Counsellors who, in most Day 
Camp situations, have direct respon¬ 
sibility for the Camp programme and 
in effect are the most important people, 
outside of the campers themselves. 

Having hired a staff with varied 
backgrounds and experience, different 


personalities, different ages, etc., how 
do we weld them into a functioning 
unit? The most successful method I 
have seen in operation, involves each 
Counsellor to the full extent of his or 
her capabilities, both in planning and 
carrying out the training course. These 
simple direct questions, “what do you 
want to know about Day Camp?”; 
“what will help you do a good job?” 
will produce more than enough discus¬ 
sion material to keep you going for 
three training courses. Naturally, 
priorities will have to be worked out. 

The following is an outline that has 
proved to be fairly successful. It is 
hoped that it might be of use as a guide 
to those responsible for developing a 
training course. 

BACKGROUND MATERIAL 

What is Day Camp: Include some¬ 
thing by way of definition, as well as 
comparison and contrast with resident 
camps. 

Reasons for growth and development 
of Day Camping: Give an historical 
outline of growth of the movement 
plus some specifics such as:—crowded 
city streets — hot summer months — 
limited opportunities for outdoor ex¬ 
perience due to finances, both of agen¬ 
cies and parents — the potentialities 
for good agency programme inherent 
in a Day Camp setting. 

Philosophy and Objectives: Point 
out here that camp attempts to provide 


26 


Canadian Camping 


the valuer, (spiritual, mental and physi¬ 
cal) of, a meaningful outdoor experi¬ 
ence, by providing opportunities for: 
learning to know and understand 
nature — learning how to live with 
others and to appreciate differences— 
developing friendships and making 
decisions—learning new skills, all of 
which is of prime importance to the 
youngsters. An attempt should be 
made here to interpret the reasons for 
and benefits of using small groups in 
the Camp setting. 

Providing this background material, 
in most cases, will be the Director’s 
responsibility. Some of it will have to 
be by the lecture-type method, but here 
he has a real opportunity for setting 
the tone for the rest of the course, by 
using the best group discussion 
methods, role-playing and buzz sessions 
(if the group is large enough). 

ADMINISTRATION 

Many of the factors here (fees, 
budget, period of operation, personnel 
policies, etc.) that have been pre¬ 
determined by the Camp Committee, 
should be interpreted by the Director. 
Other areas, such as camp routine, the 
kind of records to be kept and the 
reasons for them, attendance sheets, 
daily report forms with an outline of 
programme and problems, staff meet¬ 
ing time, managing children on and off 
transportation, campers’ councils and 
the pattern of the Camp Day can be 
discussed and agreed on by Camp 
Staff. 

HEALTH AND SAFETY 

Because this is so important, it 
warrants special consideration. Some 
of the factors to be considered are the 
use of drinking water, garbage disposal, 
personal hygiene of campers and staff, 
medical examinations, first aid training 
(bring in an expert for this), nearest 


medical help, etc. Many of the con¬ 
cerns for health and. safety relate 
directly to program andf will likely 
crop up many times. Some examples: 

Swimming and water safety: use of 
the Buddy system — swimming in 
known waters only — training" in life¬ 
saving techniques — use of proper 
teaching methods in s\yimming. — 
boating, etc. / 

Camp Craft: Firebuilding (who, 
where, when, and extinguishing), use 
of tools, (axes, knives, etc.) 

Proper Meals: Whether a lunch 
from home or meals on overnights. 

Exposure to Sun: Make it clear 
that programme should be planned to 
avoid excess exposure to sun and excess 
activities directly after meals. (This 
suggests story - hours, sing - songs or 
quiet games after lunch), 

PROGRAMME 

Good programme depends on compe¬ 
tent’, well trained counsellors and as 
far as the campers are concerned, camp 
is a success or failure as the programme 
appeals to them. 

I 

(continued next page) 



Toronto, Canada, April, 1954 


27 


Here is where the goals of the 
parent (“Johnnie doesn’t mix well, I’d 
like him to be with boys his own 
age”), the campers’ goal (fun and 
satisfaction), and the ^ency’s goal (a 
well-rounded experience, which will 
aid in camper growth), ought to come 
together. 

Programming is where the counsel¬ 
lors will want the most help and yet 
it is here that they can give the most 
to the training course, as often the 
best games, stories and craft projects 
come from counsellors who have agreed 
to prepare these materials for the train¬ 
ing course. I would like to suggest that 
each staff member should prepare an 
index of his sources of information, in 
order that a worthwhile guide of 
programme-aids can be developed for 
general use. 

The important thing in program¬ 
ming, and this cannot be emphasized 
too much in the training session, is to 
know the group with which you are 
working. Know their interests and 
their needs, their capabilities, their 
limitations, and be sure that your 
programme closely parallels these vari¬ 
ables. This suggests a whole session 
at least on the psychology of the age 
groups with which we are working. 
Once we have agreed that different 
age levels mean different interests and 


capabilities, then we can have all the 
counsellors accept some responsibility 
in lining-up programme ideas for these 
various groupings. This sharing of 
responsibility is important. 

Programe doesn’t just happen, it 
must be planned for and the more 
preparation given and the more 
resources used, usually the better the 
programme. 

Depending on the age level, the 
ideas for programme should come from 
the campers themselves. Obviously for 
the 7’s and 8’s their part in programme 
decisions can only be at the elementary 
level and programme can’t be too well 
organized (use singing games, music, 
simple crafts, water play, low organiza¬ 
tion games, etc.). This necessitates 
much programme demonstration with 
this particular age group. As we go up 
in age scales, we can expect more ideas, 
more interest in higher-organized indi¬ 
vidual and team games, a growth in 
competitive spirit, a keen desire to 
develop physical skills, and a broader 
interest in Gamp Craft, fishing, and 
water programme (canoeing, swim¬ 
ming, diving). With older boys (13 to 
14 years) much of the programme will 
be spontaneous and self-initiated. A 
good leader in this situation must be 
flexible and able to adapt equipment 
and situations.

As we pointed out earlier, most 
counsellors want specific helps. Here 
are a few that have come out of our 
training sessions: 

What do we do on a rainy day?:— 
Crafts are unlimited—have the group 
develop and present a skit—sing-songs 
are popular—^movies are always inter¬ 
esting—try relays and circle games if 
facilities are available — what about 
charades ? 

Special Events; These greatly add 
to the interest of the on-going program, 
help tie all the groups together and 
develop a camp spirit. They provide 
ample opportunity for group decisions 
and participation. How about a Penny 
Fair—^Jamborees with other camps— 
Parents’ Nights (good for community 
interpretation) — over-nights — Inter¬ 
national Days—^Junior Olympics, etc. 

Trips: These are limited only by the 
resources of the community and the 
neighbouring areas: Parks—Museums 
—Art Gallery—Nearby Fishing spots— 
Factories — Hiking Area — Places of 
Historical Interest, etc. 

Use of Natural Resources: Wood 
i^arving—wooden whistles—drift-wood 
table pieces—feathers for headdresses. 
What about a lean-to to shelter us 
when it sprinkles a little? Tadpoles 
are fun to watch and so are ants. 



Group Games: Any library will have 
scads of ideas for both quiet and active 
games with all ages, but your best bet 
is the campers themselves. They know 
dozens and dozens, and involving them 
will further point up that this is their 
camp. 

Grafts: Camper’s age usually deter¬ 
mines his dexterity and interest in 
crafts, and programme should vary 
accordingly. Clay modelling and paint¬ 
ing are popular. Wood-carving for the 
older boys (what about a big totem 
pole for the council ring?). 

Thinking in general terms, some of 
the following factors should be con-

Are you looking for new ideas to 
improve your camp? Do you want 
some help with planning a building, 
installing a chlorinator, building a 
septic tank? Do you know how many 
sources of free information there are 
on these subjects? Perhaps the follow¬ 
ing ideas will be of some help: 

Books on campsite development are 
rather scarce, but these are recom¬ 
mended: 

U.S. Dept, of the Interior, ‘^Organ¬ 
ized Camp Facilities” 

Boy Scouts of America, “Camp Sites 
and Facilities” 

Julian Salomon, “Camp Site De¬ 
velopment”, Girl Scouts of America. 

John Ledlie, “Layout, Building 
Designs & Equipment for Y.M.C.A. 


Camps”, Association Press 

Rodney Britten, “Handbook on 
Camp Architecture”; Judson Mason, 
“Cabins, Cottages and Summer 
Homes”; Barnes Swanson, “Log 
Cabins”, Macmillan 

R. Alice Drought, “A Camping 
Manual”, Barnes 

American Camping Association, “If 
Your Camp Protected Against Acci¬ 
dents?” 

In the above books you will find 
answers to a great many questions, and 
general information about a variety of 
topics in the campsite development 
field. But if you need more specific 
help, there are many other sources to 
which you can turn.

Safety Pius 

A. J. Esling 


WeVe tried Kapok and rubber, 
balsa wood and air cases and numerous 
other devices in the prevention of 
accidents on our lakes. We’ve found 
that some simply cannot take long 
usage; others disintegrate almost as we 
use them. But now the plastic chemist 
comes to our aid with a product which 
puts old-style buoyant materials to 
shame. 

In their major concern for complete 
waterfront safety, camp directors will 
turn to this new foam plastic, more 
buoyant than cork, called Aer-O-Buoy. 
It remains completely stable for its life¬ 
time, is fire-resistant; and what’s more, 
can be easily shaped or fabricated by 
the amateur in his home or camp work¬ 
shop if he is so talented. 

Last summer a great many camp 
directors saw its possibilities and ex¬ 
perimented with this wonder fabric, 
used it as flutter boards, lake markers 
and floats, arid in testing it came up 
with ideas for other uses . . . paddle 
boards, ring buoys, life belts, life rafts, 
marker buoys and boat fenders. 

A new 18-inch ring buoy has been 
approved for Red Cross water safety 
equipment. It requires no paint, no 
maintenance, and can be used for 
practice indoors or on docks because it 
will not break down or fracture during 
such training programs. 

The new ring buoy, incidentally, is 
available not only in the traditional 
white, but also in a new safety yellow. 
Acceptance of a bright yellow ring 
buoy may meet with resistance, but in 


view of the purpose of the equipment, 
which is rescue work and life-saving, 
the increased visibility resulting from 
bright yellow will be a marked im¬ 
provement. 

The paddle board is one of the finest 
pieces of rescue equipment on the 
market, because of the speed with 
which it can be placed in the water 
and the ease with which rescue work 
can be effected. Experiments are now 
under way with paddle boards made 
from foam plastic which will stand an 
unbelievable amount of rough usage 
yet will remain fully serviceable. 
Cracks, punctures, warping and other 
problems of old-style plywood boards 
will be non-existant in this new pro¬ 
duct, the buoyant force of which has 
been tested as approximately sixty-two 
pounds dead weight; i.e.—a cubic foot 
of foam plastic is equivalent to one 
cubic foot of air case. 

Its use in blocks for air case on 
watercraft offers tremendous advan¬ 
tages in safety and low maintenance 
costs. Blocks of the material placed 
underneath the rear seat of an out¬ 
board motorboat will prevent^ sinking 
if the boat is swamped. It ivtll allow 
the operator to chain his motor to his 
boat with complete safety. Gasoline or 
oil from the motor will not affect the 
material, nor will weather, fresh or salt 
water, rot or vermin affect the life of 
Aer-O-Buoy. Complete safety can now 
be built into any watercraft to make 
any boat virtually unsinkable. 

Slabs of the material have tremen¬ 
dous possibilities as replacement for 


32 


Canadian Camping 


oil drums in floating docks. The 
fmaterial would initially be more expen¬ 
sive for this use^ but once installed, 
it would require absolutely no main- 
psenance. Punctures have no effect on 
the buoyancy of the material. If need 
|be, Aer-O-Buoy can be left in the 
water permanently, and because it is 
so light, floating docks can easily be 
picked up in the Fall and returned to 
the water in the Spring with a niini- 
mum of effort and none of the hazards 
encountered through the use of oil 
drums. 


Finished products available now or 
in the very ne^ future include flutter 
boards; 11-foot paddle boards; 5-foot 
play boards; 30-inch and 18-inch ring 
buoys; Government approved buoyant 
apparatus for one person; Government 
approved life rafts; floats from 2^"^ 
X 2" to X 4"; marker buoys; and 
boat fenders; or directors can work out 
their own projects from bulk slabs 
25" X 52" X 3" or from half-inch-thick 
sheets. 


Editor’s Note: Any readers who have new ideas for the use of this foam 
plastic material are asked to let us hear about them. Inquiries and suggestions 
may be directed by mail or telephone to the CCA Office, 236 Bloor Street West, 
Toronto 5, WAlnut 2-0151.

Canadian Camping 













WE WENT TO NEW YORK 


Sixty-two strong were we from the 
land of the Maple Leaf ... a con¬ 
tingent proud to rally to the cause of 
the American Camping Association’s 
National Conference at the Statler 
Hotel in New York City. 

To know the Statler in normal times 
is to recognize it as a somewhat busy 
spot. Add two thousand camping 
people from all over the United States 
and Canada, and it turns into a minia¬ 
ture Times Square within walls . . . 
companionable, hospitable, a goldmine 
of information and new ideas, a meet¬ 
ing place for new friends and old, a 
natural setting for small confabs, where 
good talk abounds over a cup of good 
coffee. 

WE TALKED ABOUT . . . camp¬ 
ing, of course, and never tired of it, of 
more relaxed programmes for campers, 
of fewer regimented activities, of a new 
stress on the individual needs of chil¬ 
dren, of the marked and alarming rise 
in the instances of un-ad justed children 
in schools and camps, of the need for 
more camps in the medium price field. 

WE TALKED ABOUT ... our new 
proposal for counsellor recruitment and 
promotion, compared it with the New 
England system where one-third to 
one-half the membership uses it with 
no objection whatever to the charges 
. . the wisdom or otherwise of pro- 
iucing a camp directory only every 
two years ... a recent meeting held 
n a certain Western U.S. College 
where the speakers were representatives 

various types of camps who ex- 
ilained counselling in all its forms to 
he students . . , the seriousness of 
pereditation in Western Pennsylvania 


where member camps use the symbol 
of approval just as the Red Feather 
appears here, and where campers wear 
the “Acorn” pin to back up that 
approval . . . the deep concern over 
counsellor recruitment and the feeling 
that there is a need to raise camp 
counselling to the dignity of a profes¬ 
sion . . . the suggestion that camp 
counselling become part of the Uni¬ 
versity course, but that instructors in 
camps should, therefore, come up to 
University teaching standards. 

It took hours of hard work to find 
a few minutes when Hugh Ransom, 
Catherine Hammett, Cliff Labbett, 
Ted Yard, Irv Haladner and the CCA 
Secretary could meet to compare notes 
and make plans, internationally, for 
the future. By Saturday morning we 
came up with a few ideas which may 
well be the turning point towards a 
closer working relationship between the 
two Associations: 

Mutual exchange of complete 
national executive mailing lists was 
arranged, as well as an exchange each 
month of copies of both magazines. 
Further, we are to look into the pos¬ 
sibility of offering bulk subscriptions at 
reduced rates. 

From now on, representatives from 
either Association may attend Regional 
or National meetings in Canada or the 
United States, without special invita¬ 
tion. Registrations will be accepted at 
membership rates, and each provincial 
association in Canada is asked to join 
the nearest American Section of ACA, 
or the one which will be of greatest 
benefit mutually. 

Continued on page 36 


.^1 


~(ifvnto, Canada, April, 1954 


Talk of a film on camping, one which 
could be used for counsellor recruit¬ 
ment and promotion, and to be shown 
in the schools and colleges, gathered 
interest as it went along. AC A urged 
that CCA proceed with the script and 
photography and that both Associa¬ 
tions talk about a sponsor at a later 
date. 

It was also thought advisable to use 
the words “Affiliated with the Amer¬ 
ican Camping Association” by CCA, 
and to use “Affiliated with the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Association” by ACA. 

By the end of the sessions we were 
tired, but not too tired to fall in love 
with New York all over again . . . 
Broadway twinkling at night ... its 
contrasting side streets . . . Times 
Square in the early morning . . . 


Fifth Avenue teeming with other 
hurrying folk at noon ... its traffic 
literally inching its way along . . . but 
best of all the thrill of our own special 
United Nations session, and which 
semed suddenly to become the heart 
of the whole world. 

Of necessity this is a very brief 
resume. It cannot possibly convey the 
true value of our visit to a conference 
such as this, nor can it impart the 
pleasure all of us shared in meeting 
those whom we knew only by mail for 
such a long time. If it has opened the 
way to a broader understanding of our 
respective problems, if it stands for 
progress for both Associations, if it 
means we can work together towards 
the goal of Better Camping for All, 
then the trip has fulfilled its purpose.

THE MACMILLAN WILD 
FLOWER BOOK. Clarence J. 
Hylander and Edith Farrington 
Johnston. 

Obviously, years of preparation have 
gone into the Macmillan Wild Flower 
Book, one which may be profitably 
used as a book of reference, a work for 
study for counsellors and teachers, and 
certainly as a means of entertainment 
and learning for campers and students 
of any age. Four hundred and ten 
watercolor reproductions, exquisitely 
tinted according to their natural hues, 
appear with descriptive notes about 
each of the species. So lucid is the 
description that even young children 
could understand what is written. It 
is a work of art you will not leave at 
camp for the winter, but take home 
for perusal and enjoyment. $16.50. 
The Macmillan Company of Canada, 
Limited, Toronto. 




FACTS OF LIFE AND LOVE FOR 
TEENAGERS. Evelyn Millis 
Duvall. 

Keep this handy for those teenagers 
who are ready for a book of this kind. 
Intelligently written and lightened with 
sketches, it guides these young people 
through the pleasures and tortures of 
growing into well-adjusted adults. 
Mrs. Duvall handles her subject in a 
sound and reassuring manner. If chil¬ 
dren are fortunate in being able to 
discuss this topic with their parents, 
they will read through the book easily.

^idered in setting up a cour;^:t \vhqre 
ptossible, pre-camp training should be 
on the camp-site. This will provide 
atmosphere, allow counsellors to test 
programmes in their actual settings 
and will provide opportunity Tor new 
counsellors to familiarize^ .thenjselyes 
with the caihp-site. Traihmg should 
not cease with the beginning of camp. 
Regularly scheduled training sessions 
should be initiated (we always found 
that closing camp an hour earlier on 
Friday was popular with parents who 
want to get away on the week-end 
and it also ensured that the c^i^ngellors 
consider this training a part of their 
job). In addition to this, on-going 
counsellor supervision: helps the 
director get closer to the individual 
campers and their problems, and main¬ 
tains good staff morale by showing the 
counsellors that you are interested in 
them and their growth as persons. 
This matter of staff morale is an 
important factor and where possible, 
special “staff dos” should be planned. 
A real asset to those responsible for 
Day Camps is the fairly recent develop¬ 
ment of acceptable standards. The 
Recreation Division of Toronto Wel¬ 
fare Council, with the help of those 
in the field, have developed a fairly 
complete set of standards, which in 
themselves will be an excellent guide¬ 
line for a training course. 

Any Day Camp must be evaluated 
by the benefits that children gain in 
physical health and social and .mental 
wellbeing. This comes about as we 
provide opportunity for fun^ enjoyable 
activities and satisfying interpersonal 
relationships among the children and 
between the children and the;) adults. 
A good training course, whether it be 
for directors or counsellors, must help 
this to happen;

Can Have the Secret of Successful Camping! 


The secret lies in always keeping up to 
date with the latest ideas in 
’ organized camping. - 


Alert camp directors and their staffs read about tried and 
proved ideas in the monthly CAMPING MAGAZINE and the 
annual REFERENCE AND BUYING GUIDE issues. They 
know the danger of static thinking and obsolete ideas. You, too, 
will find these publications a never-ending source of new, usable 
ideas. Membership in American Camping Association 
includes your subscription to these publications and many more 
valuable benefits, costs $3.00 to $25.00 per year, depending on 
classification. Write for full information on membership. Or, 
for subscription alone, send $8.00 for a two year subscription 
to both the magazine and Reference Issue (one year, $5.00.)

material as in an 800-

CANADIANS 
ARE CAMPERS 

• 

JOIN THE CANADIAN 
CAMPING ASSOCIATION 

"MORE AND BETTER CAMPING FOR MORE 
AND MORE OF CANADA'S BOYS AND GIRLS" 

Services Offered: ^ 

1. National Convention In co-operation with Provincial Associations. 

2. National Magazine—CANADIAN CAMPING—published quarterly. 

3. National office to co-ordinate national and provincial projects. 

4. Access to up-to-date camping library. By mail service, 

5. A part in promoting better Minimum Standards for all camps. 

6. Parent and public education regarding benefits of camping. 

7. Active membership in nation-wide fellowship of camp people. 

Remember: Your membership in a provincial organization includes 
membership in The Canadian Camping Association 
and a subscription to "Canadian Camping".
